passage:
9:40 pm.

The mind loop is back: I'm not good enough. Meera got the lead role in the account team. I got a polite "next time." So I lay on the sofa scrolling through everyone's promotion posts until my eyes burned.

Then I made myself stop and take a notebook. Evidence of growth: I cut client complaints on my accounts by half this year. I trained two new joiners. I learned the reporting tool nobody wanted to touch. None of that disappears because I lost one seat.

Saurabh texted, "Dinner Saturday?" I said yes. I won't resign in a rage tonight. Tomorrow I'll ask my manager what the gap was, and give it a few months. If nothing changes, I'll look elsewhere with a clear head.

— Sonali

qa.q: What did Sonali list in the notebook?
qa.a: Sonali listed cutting client complaints on the accounts, training two new joiners and learning a reporting tool nobody else wanted.

qa.q: Why did Sonali stop scrolling, and what was Sonali feeling?
qa.a: Sonali was feeling not good enough and stung by comparison, so Sonali stopped scrolling and wrote evidence of growth to separate the loss from self-worth.

qa.q: What could Sonali do next about staying or leaving?
qa.a: Sonali could ask the manager what the gap was and give it a few months, then decide whether to push here or move on.

qa.q: What might Saurabh be offering with the Saturday invitation?
qa.a: Saurabh may be offering company and a break from rumination, showing that Sonali is valued outside any job title.

grounding: Sonali feels 'I am not good enough' after being passed over, separates performance from worth, lists growth evidence, and plans the next step.

passage: "Raghav, can I just talk for a minute? Don't fix it. When the promotion list came out without my name, the first thing in my head was, 'I'm not good enough. I never was.' I went home and scrolled through everyone's work updates till two in the morning. Everyone got something. I even drafted a resignation email. I'm Keerthana, I've been at this bank's analytics team four years, and I nearly quit in one night. Then, on Sunday, I made a list of what I actually did this year: three dashboards the whole region uses, two new hires trained, the audit handled. My manager said I need more client exposure. That's a fact, not a verdict on me. So here's what I'm deciding: I'll ask for client work for six months. If that doesn't happen, I'll look elsewhere. Calmly. Not at two in the morning."

qa.q: What did Keerthana list on Sunday?
qa.a: Three dashboards the whole region uses, two new hires trained, and the audit handled.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling the night the list came out?
qa.a: Keerthana felt ashamed and not good enough, scrolling until two in the morning and drafting a resignation in a rush of hurt.

qa.q: How did Keerthana separate performance from worth?
qa.a: By listing evidence of growth, treating the manager's comment as a fact about skills, and setting a calm plan to push for client work or move on.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel listening to this?
qa.a: Raghav may feel worried at first, then relieved and respectful that Keerthana has turned a painful night into a calm plan.

grounding: The protagonist feels not good enough after being passed over, then separates performance from worth, lists evidence of growth and decides calmly.

passage:
Tuesday: The team-lead announcement named Abhinav, not Kalyani. She sat in the parking lot for forty minutes, scrolling his profile and three others, each one making her chest tighter. "I'm just not good enough," she typed to herself in her notes app.
Friday: She drafted a furious resignation email, then saved it unsent. Instead she opened a new page titled "What's true." She wrote: led the vendor migration, cut report errors, mentored the interns. Next to it, what her manager had said: weaker at stakeholder meetings.
Two weeks later: She deleted the resignation draft. She had asked to present at two stakeholder meetings this quarter and booked a coffee with Abhinav to ask how he prepared. She had also decided that if nothing moved by June, she would apply elsewhere, as a choice, not a slammed door.

qa.q: How long did Kalyani sit in the parking lot on Tuesday?
What was Kalyani feeling while she scrolled the profiles in the parking lot?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and not good enough, her chest tightening with each comparison.

qa.q: What wise steps did Kalyani take instead of quitting in anger?
qa.a: She listed evidence of her growth, noted the real gap, asked to present at stakeholder meetings, learned from Abhinav, and set a calm deadline to decide.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see Kalyani's request for coffee?
qa.a: Abhinav may be surprised and a little awkward, but probably glad and respected that she asks to learn rather than resent him.

grounding: The protagonist, passed over, feels not good enough, then separates worth from performance, lists growth and decides calmly whether to push or move on.
